frameworks.name: Coal Fire Relationship Model
frameworks.definition: A relationship anchored in mutual respect and shared decision-making where disagreements surface from information asymmetry rather than conflicting values; initial response to disagreement is curiosity about missing information.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi lost everything twice within a 12-month period at age 26-27 (different calendar years, same age), met his partner Layla during the successful interim phase, then lost it all again. The sequence was: built business → lost everything → rebuilt → lost everything again → rebuilt again.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: occurred across two different calendar years but same age

claims.text: Hormozi forced a software company startup into existence while already managing a supplement company and Gym Watch, against Layla's explicit objection that the organization was too spread thin. The distraction cost more than the entire alternative path: had he continued investing in existing businesses instead of fragmenting focus, he would have earned more money than he lost on the subsequent sale of Gym Launch and Prestige Labs to fund the new venture.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: already managing multiple established revenue-generating businesses
single founder trying to drive multiple P&Ls simultaneously
claims.mechanism: Fragmenting founder attention across competing businesses diverts compounding effort from the highest-return venture; the opportunity cost of founder time exceeds the value of the new initiative.

anchors.value: negative ROI, lost money on exit
greater cumulative profit from concentrated growth

bounded_by: applies to service/product businesses where founder is a constraint
does not apply when new opportunity is sufficiently larger than existing combined revenue to justify reallocation

claims.text: In relationships anchored in mutual respect (Hormozi and Layla), initial response to disagreement is to ask for missing information ('what information do you have that I don't have?') rather than defending the initial position, because both parties optimize for the same goal and share similar values.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: both parties optimizing for same goal
claims.mechanism: When disagreement arises in value-aligned partnerships, the disagreement signals information asymmetry, not conflicting goals. Curiosity about the other's viewpoint surfaces the missing data.
bounded_by: does not apply to relationships where core values are misaligned
does not apply when one party optimizes for a different goal

claims.text: Hormozi's entrepreneurial journey has been fundamentally shaped by failures and losses. He frames himself as a product of his failures rather than his successes, and describes losing everything twice as a defining experience that changed who he is.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Market feedback and loss deliver unfiltered truth that social relationships withhold, forcing recalibration of self-perception and decision-making.
bounded_by: represents Hormozi's subjective framing of his own experience, not a causal claim about entrepreneurship universally

claims.text: When Hormozi's partner Layla objected to the software company venture with 'we are so spread thin, we cannot do this,' Hormozi's initial response was to dismiss her concern as unambitious thinking ('you are not thinking big enough'). He later acknowledged that she was correct and his forced investment into the new venture was wrong strategically.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has multiple existing revenue streams
new opportunity appears attractive in isolation
claims.mechanism: New opportunities present invisible costs (founder distraction, organizational fragmentation, opportunity cost of focused effort) while existing problems feel larger and more visible; the new venture's costs only become apparent in hindsight.
bounded_by: Hormozi acknowledges this was his 'number one sin' in his entrepreneurial career
applies when forced growth diverts energy from compounding existing strength

examples.text: Alex Hormozi met his partner Layla during a successful phase of his business. He then experienced a total loss of everything, rebuilt the business, and lost everything again—all within a 12-month period spanning ages 26 to 27. Despite these two catastrophic setbacks in close succession (technically different calendar years), he continued rebuilding and went on to establish successful ventures including Gym Launch and later software products.

Hormozi had built three concurrent businesses: a supplement company, Gym Watch, and was managing both when he decided to launch a software company. His partner Layla explicitly warned that the organization was too spread thin and could not support another major initiative. Hormozi overruled her objection, framed it as unambitious thinking, and forced the software company into existence as his 'pet project.' The software company was eventually sold, but at a loss: the proceeds from selling Gym Launch and Prestige Labs (the accumulated value from earlier ventures) were consumed by the software venture, leaving Hormozi with less capital than if he had simply continued deepening the existing businesses.

Hormozi and Layla disagreed about launching the software company. When conflict arose, they did not clash emotionally but instead approached the disagreement as a data problem. Hormozi would ask 'what information do you have that I don't have?' and Layla would respond with her perspective. Sometimes Hormozi would agree her data changed his view; sometimes she would agree his perspective was correct. The underlying dynamic—curiosity about missing information rather than positional defense—allowed both to update their models collaboratively.

practices.text: When facing disagreement with a partner, ask for missing information instead of defending your initial position: 'What information do you have that I don't have?'
Ruthlessly prune new opportunities and business initiatives that fragment founder attention away from established revenue-generating businesses.
